title: UniVLR: Unifying Text and Vision in Visual Latent Reasoning for Multimodal LLMs
claim: Prior methods interleave text and latent tokens with diffuse attention and high cost; ours unifies them for focused attention and better efficiency.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: paradigm diagram, attention heatmaps, scatter plot; pink vs blue coding
description: Three dashed-border panels with title banners. Panel (a) stacks two rows. The top row has a pink background labeled 'Current Methods'. It shows a question and image feeding an MLLM, then text CoT tokens interleaved with red dashed latent tokens, then the answer. Vision embeddings from an auxiliary image are encoded into the latents. The bottom row has a blue background labeled 'UniVLR (Ours)'. It shows text CoT and an auxiliary image rendered into one image, encoded into blue latent tokens, then the answer, with no text tokens. Panel (b) shows photo attention heatmaps. The interleaved design gets a sad face and 'sparse and diffuse attention'. The unified design gets a smiley face and 'denser, more focused attention'. Panel (c) is a scatter plot of accuracy against generated tokens with a Pareto frontier. A blue star for UniVLR sits at the top left, well above the red baselines Monet, SkiLa and CoVT and the orange Vanilla.
caption: Comparison between the current methods and UniVLR. (a) Paradigm illustration comparing the interleaved design of existing visual latent reasoning methods with UniVLR. (b) Attention visualization showing that UniVLR induces denser and more focused attention to auxiliary images than the interleaved design. (c) Accuracy--efficiency comparison on visual reasoning benchmarks, where UniVLR achieves higher average accuracy with fewer generated tokens. Best viewed in color.
abstract: Multimodal large language models are increasingly expected to perform thinking with images, yet existing visual latent reasoning methods still rely on explicit textual chain-of-thought interleaved with visual latent tokens. This interleaved design limits efficiency and keeps reasoning fragmented across separate text and vision channels. We propose UniVLR, a unified visual latent reasoning framework that treats textual reasoning and auxiliary visual evidence as a shared visual workspace. Instead of preserving text CoT as an independent inference-time path, UniVLR renders reasoning traces together with auxiliary images and learns to compress this unified representation into compact visual latent tokens. At inference time, the model reasons only through visual latents and directly decodes the final answer, avoiding both external tool calls and verbose text reasoning. Experiments on real-world perception and visual reasoning tasks show that UniVLR outperforms prior visual latent reasoning methods while using substantially fewer generated reasoning tokens, suggesting a more unified and efficient paradigm for visual thinking in MLLMs.
